content_text: re: assorted stock pitch questions (mostly about competitions)...3 things 1. too much focus on finding some "gimmick" pitch idea or "contrarian for sake of being contrarian" angle...too much focus on whether an idea is crowded or what everyone else thinks. I don't have any unique insight here aside from having done enough pitches, losing a lot, getting rejected, to where I have some sense what they're NOT looking for a judge or whoever is doing an intvw, is going to blast right thru this "surface-level" focus, and want to get right to: what research did you do? what work supports your thesis? there are no good or bad tickers, all tickers are equal, all angles are equal...u have to go a level deeper than that. 2. at the most basic level you can ask "whats being evaluated here"... its "analyst skill." what is that, a lot of things, but what carries the bulk of it is resourcefulness, scrappiness, comfort with incomplete information... the ability to not just spot a unique angle (the easy part) but then diligence it in a way that becomes convincing to the reader. it doesnt have to be "I have this unique insight which no one else on earth knows" (which is unlikely), everything is probabilities and risk/reward in L/S its always primary rsch, or value-added research (VAR), you see the same terms over decades but just applied to the same concept. is this 100% of what's being evaluated, no, but its the biggest lever by far in my humble opinion 3. a really good question has been: "I did all this work but I'm only 50 bps away from consensus + some variant view on LT/terminal value...is this enough" that's totally normal and actually sums up why a lot of teams fail IRL an analyst will do a shitload of work, arrive at a "this aint enough" conclusion, and then biases/dissonance kick in and the mind doesn't want all that work to be for naught...esp when pressured for idea velocity + ongoing flywheel of long and short trades so they start looking for ways to get 20% up or down, margins, multiples, all coming from a confirmation bias angle and not "is this what the research/data said?" every book on earth has some ideas in it, which suffer from this issue, to varying degrees but for pitch purposes...is it enough, not necessarily, but its also okay (since its the research process being evaluated more than the "20% upside") and combining several medium-level tenets (the "mosaic") can end up being medium-to-strong...ie having both ST and LT issues, backed by real work, can be persuasive even if the #'s arent bonkers END I'd go back thru some of the pitches in the QT below -- like, I'm definitely not the final say on this, compared to "what worked" over 50-100+ competition-level pitches...that data should be the best possible guide as to whether u have anything.
